 For more detailed info on the VS/VE% framework please see the accompanying maths paper in the EAS knowledge base: “The Shape-Volume Scalar” .

 The Shape-Volume Scalar (VS):
 Multiplying an airship’s three orthogonal aspect ratios yields a dimensionless number of 1 or above - a scalar - which was titled ‘the simple Shape-Volume Scalar’ (VS), or also ‘Toby’s number’. VS is a scale-invariant measure of a convex body’s isotropy. A sphere has a VS of 1, at any size. In airship envelope design, simple VS is a powerful rule-of-thumb style heuristic.
 For a compact convex body (i.e. an airship envelope) - a high VS indicates the form simply cannot enclose volume efficiently at any size. A low VS indicates the form likely encloses volume efficiently - however it may or may not be a suitable airship form - for aerodynamics etc. A conventional airship may have a VS between 20-30, while the Sunship has a VS of around 1.6. As
VS approaches 1 ‘directionality’ is lost as the shape approaches spherical. Low VS (<2) is thus a necessary, but not sufficient, design filter for a cargo airship.

 An airship must be very large! But the Sunship is the right type of large.

 ‘Ratio Airship’

 Volume Efficiency (VE, or VE%) :
 VE is defined as: the volume of a given shape at some size, divided by the volume of that shape’s minimum bounding sphere - expressed as a percentage. The given shape may or may not have a standard volume formula, and so volume measurement may require complex computation.
 VE is a companion measure to VS. Combined they provide a simple and robust framework for evaluating forms in the context of airship envelope design.

 A sphere is 100% volume efficient, at any size. The sphere couples maximally with the square cube law, by having maximum volume at unit length.
 For compact convex bodies (airship envelopes) VE% is inversely correlated with VS in a general way - e.g. a low VS shape will have a high VE% and vice versa. Therefore we assert that a feasible cargo airship, within the 400m size limit, must have a low-VS, high-VE envelope form.
 As directionality is fundamental to being an efficient cargo airship traversing long oceanic routes with adequate aerodynamic properties (a perfect sphere has a drag coefficient 10x that of a streamlined body) - we argue that the Sunship is the most volume-efficient airship form which also has useful inherent directionality.

 A conventional cigar airship form is inherently less than 5% volume efficient. Often closer to 2 or 3%, depending on the fineness ratio. Whereas - the Sunship’s volume efficiency of 53%, or more, means that the Sunship has 10-20x improved volume at any length.
 VE% falls away quickly as a 3D form moves away from being perfectly spherical - 50-60% is a very high percentage compared to most other forms. The scale invariance of the ratio-based
VS/VE% framework shows that the Sunship is volume efficient at any size, and a cigar form is highly inefficient at any size - despite the square cube law acting equally upon both.

 It’s worth noting that the Sunship’s volumetric envelope lies minimally within a set-of-3 orthogonal aspect ratios (e.g. 1.28:1, 1.21:1, 1.05:1), whereas it’s often a ‘given’ that a conventional airship can be described in a single aspect ratio (e.g. ‘a 5:1 airship’). In this way, conventional airship design can be viewed as one-dimensional, rather than three-dimensional. Historically, the generally male dominated aerostatics field appears to have had an obsession with only length.

 The pictured Sunship conceptual design has a VS of around 1.62 and a VE of around 53%.
Optimized ‘tubbier’, or slightly less streamlined variations of the Sunship envelope, or variations with a slightly lower truncation (and slightly smaller flat base area) can reach a simple VS lower bound of around 1.5, and a VE upper bound of around 60-65%. The exact balance between volume efficiency and aerodynamic properties is yet to be determined, but lies somewhere within these small ranges.

 The gömböc (Hungarian: [ˈɡømbøt͡s]) was discovered in 2006 by Hungarian mathematicians Gabor Domokos and Pieter Varkonyi, answering an earlier conjecture from
Vladimir Arnold. Their paper: ‘Mono-monostatic Bodies: The Answer to Arnold’s Question’ was highly influential in our R&D. It’s also noted that, based out of Australia, our team routinely pronounces (mispronounces) the shape’s name as gom-bock.

 By being mono-monostatic, the gömböc form must by definition have a top and bottom - as if it were a coin which is 99% heads, but which always lands on tails. In addition to this though, the classic gömböc shape also has L/R sides which are equal to each other, and front and rear ends which are equal to each other. But the sides are different to the ends, and the sides are slightly longer than any other dimension. Thus it has 6 cardinal directions and a general ‘directionality’, with the prime dimension oriented along the direction of forward travel.
 In this way, we argue that the gömböc is inherently more-or-less the optimal starting point for an airship envelope form.

 It is noted that the gömböc, as a mono-monostatic form, despite almost never occurring in nature, is a natural primordial form which has specific properties no other form exhibits. In this way, the Sunship is viewed as a nature-inspired design which wants to be built - in large part because the gömböc’s geometric properties translate so perfectly into favourable aerostatic properties, and the final Sunship design also seems aesthetically beautiful.

 We argue that the significance of gömböc based airship design is rivalled only by the near-impossibility to visualize such a design (without being familiar with mono-monostatic forms). The discoverers of the gömböc themselves said ‘apparently, mono-monostatic bodies escape everyday human intuition.’ and ‘that they are hiding - hard to visualize, hard to describe, and hard to identify.’ In the 20 years since the gömböc’s discovery, it has hardly been considered in any aerostatic or aerodynamic literature, if at all. Hiding indeed.

 The Sunship has three main changes differentiating it from a standard gömböc form - a flattened ‘keel’ base, and very slight fore and aft extensions (nose and tail). The pictured Sunship conceptual design also has pointed side additions, serving as general placeholders for the eventual form of the ducted thrust.
 The ‘nose’ and ‘tail’ help to emphasize directionality for the intended purpose of fuel efficiency, with minimal loss of volume efficiency. The truncated base combined with variable buoyancy provides the ability for static (grounded) standardized, modular or ‘ro-ro’ style payload exchange, compared to the standard gömböc’s curved base.
 And the Sunship’s volume envelope is, of course, a hollow volumetric shell, as opposed to the gömböc, which is by definition a solid, homogenous body.

 There are, apparently, infinitely many possible mono-monostatic forms, of which the
‘classic’ gömböc shape is just one. The Sunship conceptual design is thus both generally mono-monostatic inspired AND more specifically, gömböc inspired. We argue that any other low
VS, high VE% airship forms, which also have inherent directionality, will have more-or-less the same form as the patent-pending Sunship.

 The airship’s Aerostatics are the fundamental physics to which all other systems and design choices must adapt. The geometry of the Sunship then is the crux of its general aerostatic and aerodynamic properties, and other key design choices follow accordingly.

 3 - The Sunship is a ‘rigid’ or ‘rigid-geodesic’ airship. The double-curvature of the globally convex envelope allows extremely efficient geodesic strength with minimal materials. The sealed volume envelope is a ‘rugged’ combination of repeating simple rigid (compressive) elements and non- or semi-rigid
(tensile, membranous) elements. Triaxial ‘Smart Tension’ provides non-linear force redistribution and integrity to the whole envelope. The Sunship does not need a hangar.

 We assert axiomatically that any shape approaching very low VS, and high volume efficiency must be globally convex with double or compound curvature as, by definition, shape must approach spherical as VS approaches 1. Such forms may inherit the structural superpowers of curvature-based tessellation and load dispersion. Even if the global curvature is complex and non-uniform, the structure may be decomposed into a finite set of locally convex segments, each of which contributes to the overall structural integrity when assembled as a geodesic structure.

 Rigid (compressive) elements - the frame, or skeleton:
 The convex rigid framework essentially consists of a ‘dome’ or ‘bowl’ top half and a ‘plate’ bottom half, which join at a central ‘transition ring’. A large ‘spine’ runs centrally lengthwise from fore to aft, with stabilizing ‘ribs’ extending laterally outwards to port and starboard sides, and concentric rings connecting radially.

 Buckminster Fuller described geodesic
 domes as ‘the strongest, lightest and most
 efficient means of enclosing space known to
 man’ - and the Sunship’s globally convex
 but non-uniform curvature inherently
 retains some of the structural efficiency
 superpowers of traditional ‘geodesic’,
 complex-curvature based construction.

 It’s noted that convex geodesic structures
 get stronger and lighter (relatively) as
 they get larger - the geometry itself helps
 create the integrity of the structure.

 The Sunship’s convex form inherently
 eliminates the ‘lever-arm’, or fulcrum
 effects of a cigar shaped airship.

 The complex curvature of the rigid framework, counterintuitively, can be mostly composed of simple, repeating, straight line elements.

 As with conventional geodesic construction, most of the complexity is outsourced to the mathematics and modelling before construction - essentially leaving a large ‘shopping list’ of ‘simple’ but precise struts of various lengths and angles, to be assembled like a giant triangulated puzzle.

 In this way, the Sunship is particularly suited to modern computer simulation and mass agile manufacturing.

 The convex ‘dome’ top sections
 are self-supporting as radial
 ‘slices’, and can thus be
 constructed in stages from the top
 down, pre-affixing all necessary
 cabling and sensors etc.

 Top down manufacturing is
 currently envisioned to avoid the
 ‘keystone’ problem (of lacking
 self-supporting properties until
 the final ‘piece’ is connected). The
 final method is left unresolved in
 conceptual design.

 Current preferred enabling
 material is: Superwood –
 Inventwood or similar. (Stronger
 than steel, lighter than aluminium,
 heat and corrosion resistant, made
 entirely from wood). etc.

 Superwood appears to be perhaps unintentionally more-or-less the best rigid airship material ever made. Cerakote coatings etc. can complement if needed. Ideally, the rigid framework is thermally separated very well from the heated envelope interior, by using a sealed internal layer of cutting edge thermal insulation.

 It is (roughly) estimated that the majority of a full size Sunship could be built from a surprisingly few shipping containers worth of compression struts and other materials (if they were flat packed). The small component size, light weight and simplicity of the input materials is not intuitive, given the enormous size and complex double curvature of their eventual assembled form.

 Non-rigid (tensile) elements - ‘Smart Tension’ triaxial tension cables/straps:
 The triaxial ‘Smart Tension’ system serves two key functions. By pre-stressing the compression members of the convex skeleton, the system creates a tensionally-coherent and extremely strong whole frame, and it helps non-linear, dynamic forces like wind buffeting, or impact upon landing, to be distributed evenly throughout the envelope - avoiding buckling or breaking in any local area.

 The Smart Tension system is imagined like a triaxial barrel.
 Just like a barrel, the tension elements pre-load the rigid frame and ‘lock’ the form together.
They do this not just radially, but triaxially - from all cardinal directions, averaged out over the convex frame. e.g. Front to back, and back to front (longitudinally), bottom to top, and top to bottom (laterally), and side to side around the transition ring ‘waist’ (radially). Regions of the envelope which are physically distant can distribute their local forces through the Smart Tension system, passively propagated at the speed of sound across the tensioning belts or cables.

 In this way, with no internal support struts, the massive span of the envelope can be extremely resistant to uneven, non-linear, dynamic force by passively redistributing force efficiently - in addition to being self-supporting when grounded. A simple example is bouncing an egg wrapped in rubber bands.

The Smart Tension systems can help to resist the dynamic forces of:
 Landing, or collision
 Internal pressure increasing / decreasing over time (steady changes in heat and density)
 External pressure increasing / decreasing over time (changes in altitude or local weather)
 Non-linear internal buffeting (internal convection currents, payload movement)
 Non-linear external buffeting (vertical or side wind gusts)
 And, Force applied as pressure drag, while in motion.
 etc.

 Large span, fast and efficient convex construction has been demonstrated in the past.
Particularly by Buckminster Fuller’s domes, including for example the Honolulu Geodesic dome of
1957 which was assembled in 3 days. “The Honolulu Geodesic Dome was 144 feet in diameter, 48 feet high, and weighed only 39,000 pounds. The Geodesic Dome covered 18,000 square feet of floor space and cost $80,000”

 Other relevant examples include David Geiger’s ‘Cabledome’: “The Cabledome system is intentionally "underdeterminate" in order to exploit geometric redistribution of non uniform loads.
(Campbell, 1994)“, also the convex hulls and rigging of sailing ships.

 Hangaring:
 The Sunship does not need a gigantic hanger to live in. The Sunship IS its own hangar. It is self-stable when grounded, with almost all of its weight at the keel. Its convex form helps to resist the ‘tent effect’. A conventional cigar shaped airship when moored at the nose may need to weathervane and rotate around 360 degrees - meaning it needs a clear circular space, with the airship’s length as the radius of the clearing. The Sunship when grounded does not need to weathervane into the wind.
 The Sunship is a vehicle which is so large it becomes architecture when it is stationary. The
Sunship however is designed for constant ~20 year service life, the majority (>80%) of which is while airborne - comfortably able to avoid dangerous weather, and resist environmental exposure - including UV radiation, moisture and vibration, and also the forces associated with landing.

 Modern enabling materials, technologies and precision agile manufacturing bring the huge
Sunship volume envelope well into the realms of engineering feasibility. Amazingly, maybe the most relevant example of the general feasibility of the Sunship is the giant self-supporting, domelike, 360 metre length Cargolifter airship hangar, still standing in Brandenburg, Germany.

 The Cargolifter hangar - currently used as an indoor tropical resort - with measurements of
360m length, 210m width and 107m height, has a VS of 11.3 and around 21% volume efficiency. It contains approx. 5.2 million m3 of volume, enough volume for around 3000 tonnes of gross lift. (If the dome was re-constructed from ultra light materials, sealed, and heated to 500 ℃.) For the same lift a Sunship would need to be around 260m length, 100m shorter than the gigantic Cargolifter hangar.

 Non- or semi-rigid (membranous) elements - the skin, or shell:
 The volume envelope must seal or enclose the internal volume of air adequately, and is intended to have excellent insulative properties. It must be generally very light per square metre, and also generally highly resistant to environmental exposure. The thermal insulation may be a separate internal layer to the skin or shell, which may itself be several layers.

 The skin or shell can be attached to the rigid
 frame interiorly or exteriorly, in single, double
 or more layers.

 If more fabric-like, the envelope’s skin may
 have some compliance, or give, like a giant
 sail. Other potential materials are more shelllike and rigid, with less compliance.
 The exact configuration is left unresolved in
 conceptual design. Previous examples include
 rigid frame and thinly-skinned Zeppelins, and
 the ZMC-2 - a rigid-skin metalclad airship.

 Potential enabling materials include: Aero-gel or Pyrogel ultralight insulative materials, structure solar material: ‘Structural Solar – Praxis’ (lightweight, ultra-strong structural PV material), and various other modern materials including Dyneema Composite Fabric, or bio-manufactured ‘precision fermentation’ custom materials e.g. Cauldron. More ‘standard’ choices include ETFE fabric, ripstop nylon, Tedlar, Mylar etc.

 Integrated whole - a rigid-geodesic airship:
 The Sunship’s convex envelope is much more material efficient than the repeated, circumferential (2ℼr) and longitudinal (prime dimension) framing of a standard rigid cigar shaped airship. This reduction in framing weight helps increase Net lift.
 The Sunship’s constant curvature helps to resist the ‘tent effect’ - as the high isotropy of the almost-spherical form means there is no ‘lever-arm’, which is inherent in a 5:1 conventional airship design. The Sunship is a single coherent whole shell.
 The convex geometry gets relatively stronger as it gets larger - able to transfer local force more efficiently, and retain ‘coherence’ at any size - geometry itself is doing the heavy lifting. The term rigid-geodesic is chosen to emphasize the convex and coherent nature of the shell as a single whole, and to emphasize the overlap with Buckminster Fuller’s (and others) enabling prior work in the fields of convex architecture.

 In regard to enabling structural materials, and enabling technologies in general, it’s noteworthy that the Sunship and EAS project can be a leading demand driver for many current commercially available technologies which are unintentionally, or almost ‘accidentally’ ideal for airship use.
 These key enabling materials are available now, at price-parity, and have the necessary combination of being very light, very strong, UV/heat/corrosion resistant, cost-effective, highly recyclable etc., coupled with the ability to manufacture at scale. Increased demand from a large, newly enabled industry is a favourable economic scenario to foster partnerships and progress.

 The Sunship project in this way resembles an advanced Geodesic architecture project - whose goal is to build the Sunship’s specific ‘not-quite-spherical’ envelope form, at steadily increasing sizes over time, riding the wave of the square-cube law, until the giant structures are so large they want to float. Sunships will have to be produced in large numbers on huge state of the art outdoor assembly lines/sites.

 4 - Systems and payload modules are housed internally at the base (keel) of the Sunship, and are thermally separated from the heated interior. Internal payload weight is thus supported by buoyancy, avoiding ‘slung load’ physics while providing useful inertia and low centre of gravity.

 The Sunship's truncated base naturally forms a ‘stretched hexagon’ 2D floor plan. It is the only flat surface of the Sunship envelope. The keel is the interface point from which the convex
Sunship lands and performs rectilinear cargo exchange (e.g. shipping containers, rails, lanes, straight lines). The extremely strong, reinforced keel also provides general inertial resistance.

 Standardized Landing / Cargo Exchange:
 It’s important for operational feasibility that payload is not slung or winched underneath a floating Sunship. The Sunship’s variable buoyancy allows static, grounded, modular, standardized, safe, and adaptable cargo exchange - which can interface with existing portside infrastructure as much as possible. Static grounded cargo exchange eliminates many ground handling risks associated with suspending heavy loads dynamically, or landing, mooring and ballasting a conventional airship without true variable buoyancy.

 In the Sunship conceptual design, a floating ‘green barge’ system is envisioned for standardised cargo exchange. It's vital that interfacing with port infrastructure is inherent in the
Air-Shipping Service. Landing on the ground is possible but not preferred - due to the rarity of open, flat, unobstructed land near port infrastructure, and the Sunship’s preference for over-ocean cargo delivery operation. Despite the Sunship’s VTOL ability, a very large clear space would still be required. Selected specialised inland freight terminals may be used.

 The Sunship landing directly on water may be possible, but in current conceptual design is considered either as an emergency maneuver or for other special operational purposes. It is not a primary design requirement, if an external floating landing platform is available.

 A component simple floating barge could provide a stable platform for the Sunship to land on, utilising buoyancy principles opposite to the Sunship’s (using the incredible weight of seawater to create heaviness to help winch down and anchor the Sunship as a ballast). A platform though would need to passively or actively negate the effect of waves, to create a stable cargo loading environment.
 It’s envisioned that the exchange process is able to be performed with the Sunship oriented facing a minimum of 2 cardinal directions relative to the port or land infra, simplifying landing.
It’s noted that both on-water (amphibious), and on-floating platform airship landings have been performed successfully in the past.
 It is also noted that new portside infrastructure, and thus portside capital expenditure, should be avoided entirely where possible, or minimized where needed. The Sunship must function economically - and shipping is by definition a globally networked and integrated industry. A large but component simple landing platform is seen as the optimal compromise.

 Landing and Ground Handling:

 The Sunship can land on the floating barge, remove a single large standardized payload module (or several smaller modules, or individual shipping containers etc.) from its keel mechanically, and load separate pre-loaded payload modules. If needed, the Sunship can simultaneously charge its internal heat and/or batteries using mains power, and quickly begin its next journey - leaving behind a standardised payload module to be unloaded portside.
 The modest size of the Sunship’s payload - when compared to that of a huge container ship
- coupled with the high airspeed of the Sunship and efficient point-to-point routing allows a high cadence or throughput of payload modules, as fleet size increases. This is highly preferred for ports, compared to the monstrous task of unloading, warehousing, and reloading hub-and-spoke routed giant container ships.
 Longitudinal, lateral, and diagonal tension cables terminate at the strong, reinforced keel.
Two-thirds of the Sunship’s smart tension system can thus be accessed without having to ascend to the daunting heights of the radial tension straps.

 It’s worth noting also that the preference for floating barge based cargo exchange is partly due to Einsteinian General Relativity itself, which is an important factor at such large scales. (The
Sunship’s massive size simply cannot safely navigate very close to human-scale infrastructure:
power lines, trees, houses, cranes, large buildings, uneven terrain, etc. - yet, the Sunship is insignificantly small in the open air, relative to the incredible size of the ocean.)

 Payload Module:
 There are various potential configurations for the Payload Module/s. The configuration of the payload module and cargo exchange process are only considered broadly in the Sunship conceptual design. This is partly to avoid limiting potential possibilities through expectation or assumption.

 The payload is housed internally to the overall envelope, in order to be a part of the buoyant bubble, and supported by the lifting buoyant force. The payload must be thermally insulated from the heated volume of air - so it’s envisioned that the insulated floor of the thermal envelope is the ceiling of the payload cavity. It’s deemed critically important that the payload is not slung underneath the envelope - as, external to the buoyant bubble, and thus not lifted by buoyancy - where the force pathways change into a ‘slung load’, which introduces aerodynamic drag, potential ‘flutter’, and large stress on the frame attachments which must carry the full weight of the slung load.
 The payload module is envisioned as generally being a standardized weight, using ballast to assist standardisation, and a standardised size, potentially consisting of smaller sections. It is of course possible for the Sunship to lift any weight within its net lift, especially for ‘tramp steaming’ style spot markets - but standardisation can assist extremely fast cargo turnaround, which is a key element of industrial feasibility and route optimisation. The Sunship is a continuation of the container revolution.

 5 - Helium or Hydrogen lifting gases are not needed. ‘True Variable Buoyancy’, ‘Infinite
Hover’, and VTOL are achieved via the integrated aerostatic systems. The integrated aerostatic systems utilize the Ideal Gas Law and Archimedes’ Principle to provide lift via volumetric-thermal buoyancy. Or put simply: the ‘lifting gas’ is a giant, perfectly shaped, bubble of electrically heated hot air.

Integrated aerostatic systems - introduction and governing mathematics overview:

 Please see Appendix 1 for Aerostatics Key Mathematics and Calculations.

 The Sunship conceptual design uses a fairly simple set of governing aerostatic equations to calculate performance estimates with minimal complexity.

 1. The square cube law is the fundamental base, as lift is proportional to displaced
 volume.
 2. The VS/VE framework helps to define the design space of usable envelope forms -
 comparing volume efficiency to that of the perfect sphere.
 3. The ideal gas law and its density rearrangement explain the behaviour of the heated
 air lifting gas inside the envelope.
 4. Archimedes’ principle explains the buoyant force which provides lift. It can be easy
 to forget we live inside of an ocean of air. The atmosphere itself provides the lifting
 force to the Sunship.
 5. Heat Transfer is calculated using the sensible heat equation.

 5A: ‘Smart Heating’: Controls the envelope’s internal average temperature. Heat-loss is minimised generally via the Sunship’s proportionally low surface area, and via super-insulative materials. Initial pre-heat can use ground based mains power, and heat is retained during flight.

 The internal average temperature of the Sunship is raised over time, as air is electrically superheated via high surface area heat-exchangers, and convection currents begin as the superheated air disperses, cools, and sinks, to be reingested into the heaters at the base.
 A high % of heat energy is retained via the insulated envelope, meaning minimal heat losses. The Sunship’s high volume>surface area ratio helps provide thermal efficiency generally.

 Heating to the temperatures required for neutral buoyancy or net lift is best done via ground based power. Antora, Rondo or similar systems can provide renewable industrial thermal energy requirements. Industrial-scale renewable energy storage is expected to be industry standard within 15-30 year timeframes of the Sunship project.

 During flight the average internal temperature is ‘topped-up’ via the Sunship’s electric/battery system. ‘Topping up’ uses far less energy compared to the initial ‘pre-heat’.
 The Sunship retains a constant baseline of heat for a high % of its ~15+ year service life, generally at or above neutral buoyancy. The Sunship generally avoids completely cooling and reheating in standard operating procedures. State of the art AI controlled software, informed by internal heat sensors can control the Smart Heating systems with precision.
 The heat exchange system can be configured in various ways, with few or many heat exchangers. They may utilize honeycombing and form factor to increase surface area and heat transfer. They may be arranged vertically rising from the base of the envelope interior floor, potentially utilizing passive Chimney-Stack effect. The internal heated volume, for redundancy, may have segmentation, possibly embodied as horizontal layering - to prevent catastrophic loss of heated air via damage to the crown canopy.

 5B: ‘Smart Vents’: Control the Sunship’s internal pressure and airflows. The Smart Vents interface between the envelope’s interior and the exterior atmosphere. As the internal temperature rises, heated air is vented proportionally to maintain a steady internal pressure.

 A completely sealed envelope can allow for much more efficient recirculated heating, but the envelope must also have efficient air IN and OUT capabilities. The smart vent system is what allows the envelope to be ‘semi-sealed’.

 As the Smart heating system raises the average internal temperature of the sealed envelope, the internal pressure must increase (via Ideal Gas Law), as the rigid envelope does NOT expand like a balloon. The opposite is also true, and reduction in internal temperature of the sealed envelope will cause pressure to decrease. To avoid overpressure explosion or vacuum-buckling, and to reduce stresses on the envelope, the Smart vent system can expel heated air from the top of the envelope, and actively/passively ‘pull’ or ‘draw’ atmospheric air into the envelope.

 Air sucked inwards at the bottom of the envelope will passively be drawn into the heat-exchangers, be superheated, and dispersed up into the volume. The average temperature of the envelope is key, which includes various dynamic convection currents of slightly hotter and cooler air.
 The combination of atmospheric air IN and heated air OUT, in conjunction with the Smart
Heating system allows the envelope to control its internal temperature and pressure, maintaining a more-or-less constant internal pressure within safe operating ranges.
 The internal state is ever-evolving. The Sunship maintains average neutral buoyancy during flight, by ‘topping up’ lost heat, and is able to vary its internal density as conditions demand, e.g. responding to external changes in barometric pressure and temperature across several days of flight time. Slight internal overpressure may be beneficial during operation.

 Please see appendix 1c for heat-transfer calculation examples.

 6 - Efficient propulsion and drag reduction are both achieved synergistically via the integrated aerodynamic systems.

 Integrated aerodynamic systems - introduction:
 There are three key stages to the integrated aerodynamic systems, addressing the three relevant zones for drag reduction. Drag caused by the turbulent wake left after the airship (6A:
‘Smart Tail’ or Rear Mast), airflow along the body of the airship (6B: Ducted longitudinal thrust), and drag caused by pressure buildup in front of the airship (6C: Boundary Layer Ingestion (BLI).

 The integrated aerodynamic systems efficiently create propulsion and reduce drag, both passively via form and actively via key technologies. The aerodynamic systems, like the Sunship as a whole, are intended to be ‘component simple, design smart’ and take advantage of all available natural efficiencies. There are essentially only two moving parts in the Sunship, and both of them are elements of the aerodynamic systems (the Smart Tail, and the cycloidal propellers).

 Drag increases quadratically with speed (drag2), but the integrated systems are designed to reduce the cubic rate at which the required power, and thus fuel consumption, grows with speed.
(Power3 becomes Power2.6).
 Nature has provided us with a limit that can never be ‘beaten’ - but can be addressed and mitigated. Frontal pressure is ‘ingested’ as thrust intake - meaning that thrust and drag reduction are integrated. Ideally the Sunship can cruise efficiently at a modest subsonic airspeed
(100-140km/h) across oceanic distances (10,000 km+), using electric motors powered by Hydrogen
Fuel Cell - with sub-cubic power scaling.

 Integrated aerodynamic systems - governing mathematics overview:

 Please see Appendix 2 for Aerodynamics Key Mathematics and Calculations

 The Sunship conceptual design uses a simple set of governing aerodynamic equations to calculate performance estimates with minimal complexity. Due to the empirical nature of aerodynamics, some assumptions are needed before physical prototyping can verify accuracy. The two key figures are: the drag coefficient (Cd), which is assumed as 0.05, and the Vogel exponent
(V) which is assumed as 0.4. There are historical precedents for the working assumptions.
 The Sunship’s integrated aerodynamic systems have been designed to optimize these two figures, reducing a fundamentally complex problem to two tunable variables - allowing early modelling of per-ship performance and per-fleet performance (total work and potential revenue).

 Drag Coefficient (Cd):
 Conceptually, Cdacts as the baseline ‘seed’ of drag from which a body’s quadratic drag curve grows. Unlike the static, scale invariant VS, we cannot have true ‘unit’ drag, as drag cannot exist at velocity 0. But a low Cd shape will have low drag at any velocity compared to a high Cd shape. Cd is defined primarily by a body’s shape, and skin friction.

 The standard drag equation: D = ½⍴ · Cd · A · v2

 Has only one intervention point for a volume based airship with a large frontal area (A), and defined velocity (v), and that is the drag coefficient. The Sunship’s smart tail is thus designed to lower the Cd by approximately 10x, by giving the Sunship a near-optimal teardrop shaped flow profile. Shape is critical to both the Sunship’s aerostatics and aerodynamics. (See p35).

 Vogel Exponent (V):
 Drag scales quadratically as velocity increases - however the power required to overcome drag scales cubically. Although Cd can be lowered with streamlined forms, the quadratic dependence on velocity *itself* cannot be reduced - but with smart design and active systems, the cubic power requirement to overcome drag can be reduced, providing effective sub-cubic scaling.
 The effects of the Sunship’s active drag reduction systems are empirically quantified by the introduction of a single ‘Vogel exponent’ into the standard power equation.
 so: P = ½⍴ · Cd · A · v3 becomes, effectively: P = ½⍴ · Cd · A · v3 - V
 (or, P ~ v3 becomes, effectively: P ~ v3 - V)
 Increasing the efficiency of the drag reduction systems increases the Vogel exponent and thus reduces the power requirements to overcome drag as velocity increases.

 It’s worth noting the vital number here is a very small number and small range - from 0 to around 0.4 or 0.5, taking the exponential from 3 to 2.6, or even 2.5 or 2.4. Each step downwards is a massive improvement in real world efficiency and performance feasibility because it directly influences the amount of fuel needed for a trip across the ocean, and raises potential total fleet work and revenue (ton-km / year and $-ton-km / year). And, seeing as we cannot use diesel powered engines for our sustainable airship, and seeing as batteries are impossibly heavy, the design needs to offer a solution which is efficient enough for Hydrogen to be a feasible energy carrier, and fuel cell a feasible, steady state conversion device. There are no ‘engines’.

 Simulation, Prototyping and ‘effective’ Reynolds number:
 While it is impossible to predict every detail of the Sunship’s airflow without a full-scale vehicle, due to Navier-Stokes and Reynolds number limitations, modern simulation tools combined with creative physical modeling allow us to validate assumptions rapidly and at relatively low cost.

 At around 300 meters in length and 100-140 km/h airspeed, the Sunship’s airflow develops over around 10 seconds, forming a coherent, organised flow with emergent behaviours not seen in smaller craft or prototypes. However, by matching flow timescales and using low-speed wind-tunnel testing, we can capture the dominant flow behavior and validate core design assumptions quickly. This is similar to gigantic container ships, which also have coherent overall flow despite very high Reynolds numbers at scale - and are tested in miniature towing tanks.

 The goal is not perfect prediction; it is to establish correct scaling, tight bounds, and a coherent mathematical framework that guides design and strategic decisions. We argue this is
‘good enough’ for conceptual design to have achieved its purpose, and for the project to raise capital and proceed to preliminary and detailed design stages - where Finite element analysis
(FEA), computational fluid dynamics (CFD), and wind-tunnel experiments together provide a robust framework for assessing structural and aerodynamic performance - at which point greater capital raising can allow us to proceed to detailed design and the square-cube law based physical prototyping schedule efficiently.

 6A: ‘Smart Tail’ or Rear Mast: One of two moving components of the Sunship. A long, retractable, horizontal rear guyed-mast, which drastically reduces drag coefficient (Cd) by optimizing the
Sunship’s global flow profile. The Sunship’s aerostatics and aerodynamics are thus ‘decoupled’ for different frames of reference.

 The Smart Tail is a Guyed-mast inspired telescoping/retractable tail, or mast, which extends from the rear of the Sunship as ‘aerodynamic mode’ and forward flight begins. The tail and its guy-lines help shape and direct rear airflow, which would otherwise separate and create drag, into a near optimal ‘teardrop’ geometry for coherent low drag flow. The Smart Tail can also help provide global stability via inertia. The Smart Tail can provide meaningful drag reduction and aerodynamic stability, with no moving parts other than itself.

 Although large in scale, the structure is mechanically component-simple. Consisting mainly of a single-degree-of-freedom extendable mast stabilized by tensioned guy lines, which can be incorporated into the overall Smart Tension mesh. The Smart Tail’s robustness comes from routing dynamic, non-linear forces through tension cables, and permitting controlled elastic motion, rather than attempting to resist force through stiffness.

 By physically changing the shape of the Sunship, the Smart Tail directly affects the drag coefficient - as airflow only ‘sees’ the teardrop shaped Sunship. A standard measure of Cd for a near spherical body is 0.47, and for a teardrop, or ‘streamlined’ shaped body may be around 0.05 or less. We assert that the introduction of this large, mechanically simple component is necessary, in order to achieve this critical 10x Cd reduction.

 Conceptually, the Smart Tail is outside of the Sunship’s aerostatic VS bounding sphere - because it is retractable. The Sunship has ‘adaptive geometry’ and has essentially 2 bounding spheres. As small as possible for aerostatic mode, with the tail retracted, and as large as needed for efficient aerodynamic mode, when deployed. See page 13 - ‘ratio airship’.

 According to the VS/VE framework, the VS bounding sphere = local relativity. In this way, the Sunship is a (very significant) length (x) in aerostatic mode, when relative to buildings, trees, port infrastructure, power lines, etc., yet it is an insignificant length (x + tail) relative to the open ocean and open skies, where the vast majority of its working life is lived. The standard length of the Sunship (e.g. 300m) is always given with the tail retracted, in aerostatic mode.

 The Smart Tail is the system which decouples the Sunship’s aerostatics and aerodynamics.
Decoupling in this sense allows the Sunship to be an airship which has two shapes - one aerostatically very efficient shape and one aerodynamically very efficient shape. A single conventional envelope shape cannot have, or cannot be, both, simultaneously.

 Proportionally increasing the envelope length, or making the Sunship ‘skinnier’ or more streamlined, to lower the drag coefficient and reduce frontal area, destroys the precious orthogonal aspect ratios of the envelope, which allowed volume efficiency and meaningful lift within the 400m size limit in the first place. Adaptive geometry via the Smart Tail is thus a key conceptual design step which allows operational feasibility for cost effective, long range, heavy cargo delivery.

 6B: Ducted longitudinal thrust: Longitudinal, semi-circular ducts, containing non-combustion based air acceleration powered by Hydrogen fuel cell. Cycloidal propellers in the sealed ducts act upon a single coherent large-area mass flow, providing efficient thrust with low disk loading and no mounting pole drag.

 It’s possible to achieve great efficiency for a gigantic airship at the modest desired cruising speed of around 120 km/h, but traditional propulsion systems are not optimized for this regime.
 The Sunship’s Longitudinal ducted thrust is different to the large external air screws of historical airships, or modern ring-of-fans style distributed thrust arrays, both of which only act upon thin slices of air, requiring huge RPM and causing mounting pole drag.

 Propulsive efficiency for a large, slow airship is governed by momentum theory, with thrust given by F=𝑚˙ Δv. Minimizing induced power therefore requires maximizing mass flow rate
(𝑚˙) while keeping velocity increment (Δv) small.
 The Sunship wants fewer, giant propellers moving a huge amount of air at a gentle speed - as opposed to more, smaller propellers moving a small amount of air at a high speed. By housing the propellers in a sealed duct, oriented in the direction of travel, we are stabilizing the airflow, and effectively increasing the size of the propellers - by acting upon a single giant coherent mass flow.
 The aerodynamic low-profile ducts eliminate mounting pole drag, and encourage coherent external airflow along the body of the Sunship - their gentle curvature encouraging boundary layer attachment passively via the Coandă effect.

 In the Sunship’s conceptual design, there are 4 main thrust ducts - L/R sides, both high and low. The propellers can also reverse their direction of thrust.

Cycloidal (radial wheel) propulsion:
 Despite being a fairly well proven technology, particularly utilized in marine environments, cycloidal propulsion is practically unused currently in aerodynamic environments - failing in the extreme blade speed and high Δv requirements of helicopters or planes.
 Cycloidal propellers however are uniquely suited to the hull-integrated ducted airflow architecture of a giant Sunship with moderately low airspeed. It is already established that housing many large propellers inside of long ducts is preferred for efficiency reasons.

 Traditional axial propellers must be housed in circular ducts, a terribly inefficient geometric fit to attach externally to a large convex body. If the circular ducts are changed to semi-circular, so as to lower their profile, the maximum blade length (rotor diameter) to fit inside the new duct shape collapses, disk loading rises, mass flow falls, and efficiency degrades sharply.

 Wheels, however, avoid this geometric trap by spinning radially, and thus sweeping laterally ‘along’ the direction of flow. (Rather than spinning axially, and sweeping perpendicularly to the direction of flow.) This allows a large effective actuator disk (very large fan blades, acting as wheels) to be embedded in semi-circular or flattened low-profile ducts. The ‘swept width’ can be made huge without increasing the duct profile dramatically. This preserves the low Δv, high-mass-flow regime that a slow, buoyant, 300m airship requires for efficient long-duration cruise, and maintains the low VS needed for aerostatics.
 Breakthrough Sunplower cycloidal ‘radial wheel propulsion’ is an example of a perfect enabling technology and potential strategic partner.

 The propellers are the second moving part of the sunship.

 Although large megawatt-class cycloidal propellers have not yet been built, there is no physical barrier to scaling. Blade RPM falls rapidly with size; and tip speeds can remain well within material limits. Pitch-controlled blades at comparable or larger scales already exist in wind-turbine engineering, making 5-10 m propellers with MW scale input power entirely plausible.

 Fine Control System - The Illusion of Total Control
 The Sunship has direct control of 3/6 Degrees Of Freedom (DOF), which is one more than a car’s 2/6. A shopping trolley has direct control of 3/6 DOF, but they are not the same 3 as the
Sunship. The Sunship’s 3 DOF is less than the maximum 6/6, which some submarines can achieve.

 The car drives on top of the road, but also through the atmosphere. Most of the car never actually touches the road, only a very small segment of each tyre at any one time, over time.
 The Sunship drives through the atmosphere, while floating, entirely immersed inside of it. The
Sunship’s road is the atmosphere, and all of the Sunship’s exterior is in contact with the atmosphere, at all times.
 The submarine also drives through, and floats inside of its environment, but the submarine’s environment (the ocean) is 800x the density of air.

 The Sunship has direct control over 2/3 translational Degrees of Freedom - ‘heave’
(vertically rise and fall along z axis via aerostatic lift), and ‘surge’ (forwards and reverse along x axis via thrust or reverse thrust).

 The Sunship also has direct control over 1/3 rotational DOF - ‘yaw’ (left or right rotation around z axis). Yaw control is achieved via uneven thrust between the left and right hand side propulsion tubes. As the cycloidal propulsion can operate in reverse, it therefore helps to think of the Sunship as ‘driving’, and of the propellers as left and right hand side ‘wheels’. The Sunship can yaw ‘on a dime’ around its center.

 During landing procedures, with minimal or no airspeed, yaw can provide ‘turning on a dime’, or close to. The use of guide lines attached to weighted ocean barges can help to stabilize the
Sunship as it is ‘reeled’ in, during landing procedure. Active sway control (horizontal ‘strafe’ movement along y axis) is thus considered effectively redundant.

 The Sunship is imagined as having only partial, or ‘reactive’ control of 2/3 rotational DOF -
‘pitch’ (nose up or down rotation around y axis) and ‘roll’ (sideways rotation around x axis). The
Sunship can also partially resist horizontal ‘sway’. This is similar to a ship, which is constantly pitched and rolled by the waves, but whose rudder only controls port and starboard heading.

 The inertia of the heavy payload can resist sudden gusts of wind or abrupt changes in local external barometric pressure, (which may only affect one side or section of the Sunship). The low centre of gravity helps ensure the Sunship ‘wants’ to stay upright and return to stable equilibrium.
The payload itself can act as a tuned mass damper, similar to those used in skyscrapers to resist earthquakes (which happen very rarely). The Sunship is, however, a flying skyscraper. So it is constantly subject to dynamic forces during flight.

 The Sunship has a generally defined use case and a finite service life, and ultimately a defined set of regular flight maneuvers. Due to the gigantic size - nimble or precise movement close to land infrastructure or other Sunships is preferably avoided entirely, and a Sunship can perform its long, lonely cargo journey ideally almost unsighted.
 It’s argued that direct control of 3 DOF, plus inertial stability in 2 other DOF, combined with a guide-lined based ‘reeling in’ landing procedure, provides enough maneuverability and dynamic stability to complete standardised takeoff and landing, and long distance cruising, and thus perform the Sunship’s main task of long distance cargo delivery, without the need for specialty fine control systems.

 6C: Boundary Layer Ingestion (BLI): BLI intakes are incorporated into the frontal form (nose)
and sides of the Sunship. BLI lowers pressure drag with increasing efficiency as velocity increases.
Integrating thrust and drag reduction reduces the Sunship’s expected power consumption drastically.

 It’s noted that the frontal BLI and general flow pre-conditioning is intentionally left as the
3rd element of the integrated systems, not the first. Counterintuitively, most of the drag on a moving body arises from the rear low-pressure wake created by turbulent flow separation behind the moving body - not just the body ‘pushing’ into the air in front.
 This rear wake effectively ‘pulls’ on the moving body as it separates. Because flow is motion through time, the rear wake ‘talks to’ the frontal flow at the speed of sound, and the pressure field evolves globally. It seems as if what happens after the airship influences what happens before the airship. This ‘feels’ different to our everyday human experience. In the Sunship conceptual design, we have addressed rear-wake first, thrust and longitudinal flow second, and left frontal drag reduction via BLI until last.

 Boundary Layer Ingestion:
 The propulsion system utilizes Boundary Layer Ingestion (BLI), drawing intake air for the longitudinal propulsion directly from the airship’s ‘frontal pressure drag’ zone. Like opening a door from the inside while somebody is pushing on it - air particles, or ‘packets’ which would potentially become frontal pressure drag, or aft-body separation drag, are efficiently ingested into the thrust tubes and accelerated, becoming thrust, and recovering some of the potential lost momentum. This system is encompassed by the Vogel exponent.
 BLI not only reduces overall drag but also compounds mass flow efficiency, creating an efficiency gain that increases with velocity over the operating range, i.e. BLI is more effective as speed increases, optimized for the Sunship’s preferred cruising speed.

 Integrated Thrust and Drag Reduction - Overall Design Justification
 The Sunship’s large but component simple Smart Tail reduces the baseline Cd by around
10x. The Sunship’s ducted longitudinal thrust utilizes the enormous curved length of the vehicle for efficient coherent thrust with no external mounting drag. The BLI drag reduction systems recover part of the momentum deficit that would become frontal pressure drag, thus lowering effective drag as velocity increases.
 This effectively reduces the coefficient in the cubic power law (quantified by the Vogel exponent), ideally improving fuel efficiency at cruising speed (~120 km/h) enough for Hydrogen fuel cell to be viable. Green Hydrogen Fuel Cell is the optimum energy carrier choice and is more-or-less non-negotiable, when deep sustainability is recognised in the overall project scope.

 In contrast - external diesel airscrews or distributed electric thrust arrays act on thin, independent, non-coherent slices, or packets, of fresh air. They move smaller, faster air masses, meaning higher Δv and lower efficiency, and they do not ingest the boundary layer - meaning that higher velocities require higher power with standard cubic scaling.

 Early windtunnel examples of the ‘useful directionality’ of the Sunship’s shape, and Smart-Tail, in comparison to the turbulent aft-flow of a regular sphere. Top: Sunship’s pronounced ‘teardrop’ flow profile, and notable lack of separation, compared to sphere’s turbulent aft flow. Bottom: lines 1-3 are laminar for
Sunship, across entire length of wind tunnel, with lines 4-6 partially turbulent. In the sphere, only line 1 remains laminar for tunnel’s length. Line 2 is partially turbulent, 3-6 fully turbulent. BLI is not modelled.

 7 - The Sunship can uniquely collect unlimited fresh atmospheric water and sunlight.
 Please see appendix A-3 for water collection calculations.

 Fresh water is, in principle, about as unlimited as solar energy, despite being so precious, and increasingly so dangerously scarce in much of the world. Current global groundwater depletion is around 200-300 trillion litres per year (300 km3), or around 0.5-0.8 trillion litres per day, a staggering amount! This is the critical, non-replenishable groundwater, geographically linked to the water crisis, and ‘post-crisis’ water bankruptcy. The total global planetary water usage is around 4000 trillion litres per year (4000 km3).
 Earth’s total hydrological cycle however makes human requirements seem miniscule. In total the cycle moves an enormous ~500,000 trillion litres of water per year (500,000 km3) as rain or snow. The current global groundwater depletion is less than 0.1% of the total fresh atmospheric water available, if only that water could be efficiently collected and transported.

 The global water cycle is driven by solar-powered evaporation, providing an effectively endless atmospheric water supply. Over 90% is simply a closed ocean → raincloud → ocean loop.
There is no physical limit preventing the sustainable collection of huge amounts of atmospheric fresh water from above the oceans, for hundreds or even thousands of years - and even to eventually achieve global fresh water surplus, and begin to refill Earth’s depleted aquifers.
 It is important to note that any atmospheric fresh water that is collected - whether as caught rainfall, or condensation, is continuously replaced almost instantly by evaporation from the oceans, in international waters. The scale of this evaporation is enormous, and solar-powered, making the atmospheric supply functionally inexhaustible on human timescales.
 The entire planetary hydrological cycle, though giant when compared to human requirements, moves only around 0.0003%, or 1/2700th of the volume of the water in Earth’s oceans themselves (1.33 billion km³). Hydrological Earth can be achieved by diverting one
2.7-millionth (0.000037%) of the planet’s total water, caught just before it landed back in the salt-water oceans anyway. The vital fresh water can be diverted through all necessary human and environmental uses, efficiently, before that water returns back to the cycle - absolutely insignificant in scale the the cycle itself.

 Persistent offshore interception of high-intensity precipitation systems within equatorial convergence belts allows Sunships to harvest large freshwater fluxes when rainfall is strongest.
For maximum annual throughput, water is constantly cycled rapidly to the nearest coastal hubs.
 Fresh water pipelines and standard truck/train infrastructure from coastal ports can help deliver the majority of collected fresh water inland - saving the water collecting fleet having to travel excessively large distances, reducing cycle time.Alternatively, longer-range deliveries to key drought or humanitarian zones can provide high-impact strategic relief where it is most urgently needed.

 Airship based atmospheric fresh water collection at scale is an extremely important technical possibility, of equal commercial and humanitarian importance to Air Shipping as a
Service. Atmospheric water collection can address both critical humanitarian and environmental concerns around fresh water - and also the scaling up of global green Hydrogen production, which requires ultra pure fresh water as an input.

 All other general increases in water use efficiency are of course directly beneficial.

 Solar Collection:
 Please see appendix 4 for solar collection calculations.

 The Sunship’s non-propulsion
 systems are powered by the smart
 onboard batteries, which can be
 recharged during flight via
 photovoltaic solar collection
 technology.

 Thin, light, flexible and highly
 resistant PV technologies already
 exist which can perform this
 function, or structural solar
 panelling allows PV technology to
 be incorporated into the shell itself.

 Despite the proportionally low
 surface area, the Sunship still has a
 massive amount of surface area for
 solar collection. If needed, the
 batteries can be recharged during
 cargo exchange with mains power.

 Other systems and softwares (brain, sensors, telemetry etc.):
 Autonomous ‘auto-pilot’ software can control each individual Sunship. As airships are affected by both aerostatic and aerodynamic physics simultaneously, they are never completely
‘stable’ and their flight condition is ever changing. They are thus perfectly suited to auto-pilot, constantly making changes to the Sunship’s state based on data at various rolling-average time scales.Onboard pilots or crews are possible but not envisioned. The Sunship cruises well under the flight path of commercial airlines.
 The Sunship’s unique characteristics and role provides opportunities for innovative software stacks. Onboard sensors can gather data such as: internal average temperature and pressure changes over time, total gross lift, net lift and buoyancy, forces acting upon the envelope, wind speed and direction, weather patterns, Sunship speed, direction, battery %, PV charge rate etc. This data can be fed to Smart systems e.g. actuators tightening or loosening Smart Tension,
Smart Heating changing buoyancy, altering the length of the Smart Tail etc.
 Also, at a fleet level, inter-agent communication can help to continually optimize Sunship routes and avoid collisions. The Sunship fleet can offer on-chain, dynamically priced ‘tramp steaming’ spot market services, and regular-service routes. The routes can integrate into regulated carbon-credit exchange platforms, generating accredited carbon offsets per-flight.

 8 - Sunship technology can scale to meet and exceed global ton-km per year demand.

 The Sunship is inherently a fleet based design. Significantly less Sunships over the ocean can gradually displace all current merchant marine in the ocean. Despite the audacious size of the project, there appears to be no physical limit preventing the eventual decarbonisation of the global shipping fleet, or the offset of all global groundwater use. To try for yourself visit the interactive
‘EAS Fleet Calculator’ in the EAS knowledge base.

 “Let’s say airships captured half of the 13 trillion ton-km currently served by container ships at a price of 10¢ per ton-km. That would equal $650 billion in annual revenue for cargo airships, notably much bigger than the $106 billion Boeing reports for the entire global air freight market. If one company owned the cargo airship market, taking only half of only the container market, it would be the biggest company in the world by revenue.
 How many airships would we need to fill that demand? A lot. If each (388m long) airship can carry
500 tons, cruises at 90 km/h, and is utilized two-thirds of the time, that adds up to around 260 million ton-km per year per airship. To produce 6.5 trillion ton-km per year would require 25,000 such airships.
This is about the number of airliners in the world today.” - Eli Dourado, 2023

 The hypothetical airship in Eli’s article is used as a good reference for a ‘conventional’ design, and 25,000 airships is thus used as an arbitrary ‘line’ of feasibility for a maximum fleet size.

 If, instead, each Sunship (standard, only 300m long) can carry 4,767 tonnes, cruises at
120km/h and is utilised 81% of the time, that adds up to around 4.05 billion ton-km/year per
Sunship. To produce 6.5 trillion ton-km/year would require around 1,600 such Sunships. This is
15-16x more yearly work per airship, with each Sunship around 88m shorter in length.
25,000-30,000 such ‘standard’ Sunships could perform the work of the Earth’s entire maritime shipping demand, currently serviced by the global merchant fleet of around 100,000 ships.

 If each Sunship was instead an extra large 388m long, the length of the conventional 500t design (i.e. gigantic, potentially at the upper limits of operational feasibility), they could carry around 11,150 tonnes each, over 20x that of the conventional airship design. To service half of the container market would take only 685 such XL Sunships. A fleet of 25,000-30,000 of such extra large Sunships could perform around 240 Trillion ton-km/year of work. Enough to service over double the current entire maritime freight market, or, enough total work to service the global maritime freight market and global atmospheric fresh water demand (for environmental and humanitarian uses, green H2 production, etc). This is all while avoiding Helium or Hydrogen lifting gases, and potentially entirely sustainable, with recyclable, non-toxic input materials.

 With these vastly improved projected performance figures, EAS has the capacity to become one of the largest companies in the world by revenue. The breakthrough design has a uniquely uncapped and inspiring potential due to its scalability.
 The scalability of the Sunship design allows a reimagining of the future, which can be prosperous, global and futuristic, yet non-toxic, non-carbon emitting, equitable, beneficial, and sustainable, in harmony with nature and planet Earth.

 FAQ

Why now? Why not 20 years ago?
 A few reasons: The gömböc was only discovered in 2006, and the VS/VE framework and
Sunship conceptual design only completed around 2024-25. Modern processing power means we can perform static and dynamic style simulation and modelling, and modern materials and manufacturing are already incredible and getting better. CO2 emissions are rising. The Sunship’s time has arrived.

How much will a Sunship cost?
 As a benchmark: existing container ships and cargo jet airliners can cost in the tens, to hundreds of millions per vehicle. The Sunship is expected to be surprisingly cost effective at scale, despite their huge size - as they are mostly empty space and have minimal moving components.
““I think a modern Zeppelin could be built for less than ten million dollars.” - Casey Handmer

Can the Sunship carry passengers?
 Technically, yes, of course, a Sunship could carry almost anything. In practice - no, over ocean cargo is the main priority.

Can the Sunship fly over land?
 Technically, yes, of course, a Sunship could fly almost anywhere. In practice - over-ocean cargo is the main priority. Specialised, optimised over-remote-land, over-peninsula, over-land, or over-mountain routes could be organised with support from governments.

What about regulations?
 The Sunship will need to pass all requisite regulatory unmanned requirements, operating at the highest operational and engineering standards, as comparable existing industries already do.

What about ground crew or flight crew?
 It is also noted that airships are by their nature almost never in a steady equilibrium - they are constantly moving, their state is constantly changing. Airships are affected by both aerostatic and aerodynamic physics simultaneously. Therefore airships are uniquely suited to modern digital autopilot control, and empirically informed LLM learning.

 There will need to be ground crew specialised in the Sunship’s unique requirements. We expect that the Sunship will be far safer and more standardised than any other airship to handle.
Ideally flight crew will be either not needed or minimally needed, as the Sunship, and airships in general, are perfect candidates for autopilot - as they are subject to both aerostatic and aerodynamic physics simultaneously, and are essentially never, or rarely, in a stable equilibrium, needing constant minute adjustment. EAS will eventually need large teams of specialist employees in many fields, in the same way comparable industries have currently.

What colour will they be?
 The top may be a dark colour of PV cells, but not necessarily so. If possible, we would like to make them as colourful as possible. The massive external surface could be used for art, promotion, etc.

What about aerodynamics? How will they be stable - or fly straight?
 Conventional airships have already successfully flown incredible distances and timespans - while managing turbulent weather, payloads, and changing course… All while literally being a giant lever, of 5 or 6:1 ratio - optimised only for forwards flight. They are however extremely fragile when static (grounded) or near-grounded. The Sunship, with integrated aerodynamic systems, and heavy keel, can be equally as resilient to turbulence generally, by being self-proportional, and using cutting edge design to achieve efficient forward flight.

What about bad weather?
 Conventional airships, around 100 years ago, have already outrun storms and successfully crossed oceans. With modern GPS and telemetry, and a comparable airspeed, the ‘ruggedised’
Sunship can easily outmaneuver bad weather patterns during flight - and will be built to withstand the various operating conditions. We don’t put boats or trucks in hangars to protect them… So why cargo airships.

Who is your customer? What is your beachhead market?
 Aggregated freight emergencies - captive customers who have no choice but to pay exorbitant air freight fees due to a missed boat. Aggregated customers who have no choice but to use airfreight despite not being a ‘good fit’ for it - volumetrically penalised customers, shipping semi-urgent products with low density. Bottleneck and chokepoint relief. Crucially - beachhead markets are aggregations of shippers, who may individually only experience a perfect scenario for
AirShipping infrequently - but as an aggregate, provide a liquid market desperate for a middle option.

I thought airships couldn’t fly straight with a fineness ratio of less than 4:1?
 A mono-monostatic (Gӧmbӧc) form is fundamentally different to a prolate spheroid of ever decreasing fineness ratio. The Sunship is envisioned as a balance of at least three fineness ratios.
The Sunship is close to spherical and self-proportional when grounded or hovering. When moving forwards during flight, with smart-tail extended, The Sunship is much closer to the ideal
‘streamlined body’ form, with BLI and longitudinal ducted thrust creating an efficient configuration. We argue that airship development should optimize low VS forms, to fly ‘well enough’ to perform useful work, with ultra-heavy cargo - rather than assuming a high VS form, with good straight-line aerodynamics, without a useful payload.

What about X conventional assumption?
 Is it right to blindly accept or follow criticism or wisdom from a field which is self-evidently unable to perform useful work currently? Penny farthing or modern E-bike, which would you rather ride daily to work?

Won’t you run out of money before they’re built?
 We argue that the EAS project can be surprisingly low risk, and surprisingly capital efficient - despite ultimately being a very large scale project. This is possible due to the square-cube law based strategy inherent in the Sunship’s physics.
 In the spirit of Pareto’s Law - a huge amount of enabling work can be done early and be surprisingly capital lean. “A project with similar unit cost to SpaceX - addressing a market 30x as large”. EAS has the potential to be addressing that market as a first mover and trailblazing company. The risk is worth the reward - so much so that, coupled with the Sunship’s uniquely strong and broad patent-pending design, the project provides many opportunities for milestone based valuation, fundraising and partnership strategies.

What about birds?
 For comparison, sadly there are millions of bird deaths annually from bird strikes with planes, mostly near airports at low altitude. The Sunship, by being gigantic and moving at a much more modest speed, is expected to be far safer for birds. The BLI intakes can be simply ‘meshed’ to avoid intaking birds, and the Sunship, despite flying much lower than planes, would still fly hundreds of meters higher than most sea birds’ flight altitudes.

Is the design finished? I think it could be better
 No, the conceptual design is exactly that - conceptual, with elements left intentionally ambivalent. There are many decisions and details to be made at the ‘edges’ of design - to be finalised in further preliminary and detailed design stages.

I’m scared of technology, doesn’t it just make things worse and destroy the planet?
 We hope the Sunship is an example of ‘design for planet + humanity’ - and that, by replacing an already existing technology with an emissions free and efficient alternative, which can harvest clean water, that the effect is a massive net positive, and inspirational for other decarbonising technologies worldwide.

Can the Sunship land on water?
 Technically they may be able to, but it’s currently envisioned as a last resort maneuver.

What if somebody shoots the Sunship with a gun? Or a rocket launcher? What happens in a catastrophe?
 Due to the Sunship’s size, and the ambient internal pressure - some small holes in the envelope would not be catastrophic, and may even be insignificant in regards to performance.
Internal segmenting can also provide redundancy. The Sunship is designed to operate either uncrewed or minimally crewed, at a modest speed, over the open oceans. We argue The Sunship is similar to, or safer than, existing tolerated risk profiles.

How will they be built?
 Rapid, low cost, outdoor additive assembly line. Because of the modular assembly of the
Sunship, and the repetitive simple components, we envision a (gigantic) assembly area which can repetitively build and attach modular segments of the Sunship from the top down, raising each segment as the new segment is built and attached underneath. It will necessarily take years to decades to build a full planetary fleet of Sunships, to gradually retire and replace much of the
Earth’s current ~100,000 ship merchant fleet as they reach the end of their service life.

Will EAS build all of the Sunships?
 EAS will likely partner with key manufacturing partners to begin prototyping and initial fleet construction as a first mover - and after the expiration of our 20 year patent, industry competition is welcomed for the betterment of the Airshipping industry and planet.

Surely it’s impossible to build something so big?
 It’s more or less already been done before! If you compare elements of the Sunship to historical or current projects, airship, maritime, architectural or otherwise. The Sunship is a reconfiguration of many generally proven elements, and the geometry itself does the heavy lifting at large sizes.

What if you collect too much water, will we ever run out?
 No, as over-ocean atmospheric water is replenished instantly by evaporation of equatorial oceans on gigantic scales.

What about all the ships in the ocean?
 The buildout of Sunships would help slowly promote a gradual phase out of certain types of ships as their work was performed instead by air. Container ships generally have around a 20 year service life. We intend the Sunship to be minimally disruptive in the short and medium term, and take a long time to reach full fleet size, in conjunction with the IMO, UNCTAD, governments and other industry bodies. It’s very possible in the future there will be significantly less ships in the ocean, in line with the IMO’s ‘by or around 2050’ decarbonisation deadline. The whales may be much happier.

Who are you going to sell the airships to?
 EAS will not be selling airships. The business model is to build and operate the Sunships to provide emissions free Air Shipping as a Service (ASaaS) for existing industry stakeholders
(shippers, carriers, and freight-forwarders) and also spot market services. ASaaS will allow stakeholders to earn carbon credits on the over-ocean leg of the cargo’s journey - and to integrate with existing portside land infrastructure. The Sunship can also provide atmospheric water collection and delivery.

I don’t like the name Sunship
 Just call them airships if you like.

What if I want to learn more? Can I join the project?
 contact@electricairshipping.com

 Appendix A - Mathematics and Calculations

 At the conceptual design stage, key calculations have been used to determine the critical scaling or limiting factors - either for a single Sunship, or at the fleet level. These factors mainly include physics based limitations, impacting power requirements and fuel requirements, but also include sustainability credentials. It is important in our conceptual design to attempt to ‘kill’ or disprove the design where possible - as it must withstand scrutiny, and ultimately, you cannot fool nature.
 It is found that, despite being an audacious scaled project - there seem to be no critical or impossible limits in the Sunship’s design, or full scale fleet operation. There is huge scope to change or improve the following calculations, and piggyback off of other enabling breakthroughs.

 However some critical assumptions are made as follows:
 A maximum desired fleet size of 25,000-30,000 Sunships is set as a limit, with two main fleets, an ASaaS fleet and an AWC fleet, and an assumption of decades of time to reach this scale.
 The key assumptions for Sunship calculations are: a 300m length ‘standard’ Sunship, with a
VE of 53%, a Cd of 0.05 and a Vogel exponent of 0.4. Small changes in these numbers can change the feasibility outcomes quite drastically. The standard Sunship can carry 4767.05 tonnes of payload, and cruise at 120km/h airspeed. A ‘tubby’ Sunship of VE 56.7% is used in section 1c.

 Slight changes to the Sunship’s VS or VE directly affect volume-per-length and Net lift.
Slight changes to the Cd or Vogel exponent can produce exponentially better or worse power (and fuel consumption) figures. The Vogel exponent alone is the key reason for the integrated drag reduction systems in the design, and allows a single integer to represent a complex empirical outcome. A truly accurate Vogel exponent can only be determined empirically at scale, but estimates can be refined greatly with simulation and prototyping.

 A very crudely estimated Sunship weight (830 tonnes at 300m length) is used in sections 1b and 1c (p51 and 52). The assumed Sunship weight can be increased, even doubled, without sacrificing feasibility, it is not an ‘exponential’ figure. Decreases in component weight however are very desirable as they directly affect Net lift.

 The Sunship fleet, acting over many decades as a huge demand driver, is a critical assumption for the scaleup of green H2 production, in section 2b (page 57). It is assumed that, over the next several decades, the planet will continue the transition towards increasingly sustainable and efficient energy capture, storage and production - especially if there is growing demand from the nascent ASaaS industry and other sectors.

 1a - Aerostatics Key Maths:

 Ideal Gas Law: PV=nRT
(P)ressure x (V)olume) = n (Amount of Substance) x R (Ideal gas constant) x (Temperature)

 The Sunship’s Internal Temperature (T) increases over time (via Smart Heating), and the
Amount of substance (n) (air) inside the envelope decreases proportionally (via Smart Vents). This means with a constant Volume (the envelope does not expand like a balloon) and constant R (Ideal
Gas Constant), the envelope’s internal Pressure remains functionally constant, within an acceptable range. Air is gradually heated and the heated molecules are vented at the same rate at which pressure increases. During cooling the opposite is true - if Temperature decreases, the amount of substance (air) must increase proportionally.

 Ideal Gas Law (expressed for Density): ⍴ = PM / RT
⍴ (Density) = (Pressure) x (Molar Mass) / (R Ideal Gas Constant) x (Temperature)

 Because Pressure, Molar mass and R (Ideal Gas Constant) are constants, raising
Temperature reduces density (⍴) directly.

 Archimedes’ Principle:
Buoyant force = Density of fluid being displaced ⋅ Gravity ⋅ Volume of displaced fluid
 The lift is proportional to the displaced ambient air volume, and depends on the difference in density between the ambient air and the heated air inside the envelope. This density difference, and thus weight difference, creates the lifting force, in accordance with Archimedes' Principle, which states that the buoyant force is equal to the weight of the displaced ambient air. Buoyant lift is provided by the ocean of air itself.
